'Did you hear about Rupa and that manager?' Jasleen asked her sister, drying the steel plates.
'Mm. Mausi told me.' Alka shook her head. 'But why did she keep going to those late meetings? Why did she let it go on for months?' She stopped, a plate in her hand. 'Wait. Listen to me.'
'What?'
'I'm asking what Rupa did wrong. She didn't make him send those messages at midnight. She didn't make him threaten her appraisal.'
Jasleen leaned on the counter. 'So what's the real question?'
'Who had the power there? He did. He chose to send them. He chose to hold her job over her head.'
Alka put the plate down. 'I'm calling Rupa tonight. Not to ask why. Just to ask how she's doing and what she needs.'
'I'll sit with you while you call,' Jasleen said.

qa.q: What did Alka say the manager chose to do?
qa.a: He chose to send the messages at midnight and chose to hold Rupa's job over her head.

qa.q: Why did Alka stop with a plate in her hand?
qa.a: She noticed that her questions were all about what Rupa did wrong, and it bothered her that she was blaming the person who was hurt.

qa.q: What did Alka decide once she changed her question?
qa.a: She decided to call Rupa that night just to ask how she was doing and what she needed, instead of asking why she let it go on.

qa.q: How might Rupa feel if the call began with 'why did you keep going to those meetings'?
qa.a: Rupa would probably feel judged and ashamed, and might stop telling her family anything about the manager.

grounding: A woman catches herself asking why Rupa let harassment continue and turns the question to who held power and chose to act.

passage: Last month my flatmate Jaya came home shaking; two men on a bike had snatched her phone outside the metro station. My first words, and I'm not proud of them, were, "Why were you holding it out on that road? You know that stretch." She went quiet and took her tea to her room. I'm Uma, and I've always thought of myself as the practical one. That night I lay awake replaying it. Jaya didn't grab her own phone and ride away with it. Two men planned it, waited for someone distracted, and chose to do it. My question had quietly put her on trial. The next morning I knocked, sat on her floor, and said, "I'm sorry. They did this, not you." Then I helped her fill in the police complaint.

qa.q: What happened to Jaya outside the metro station?
qa.a: Two men on a bike snatched her phone outside the metro station.

qa.q: Why did Uma lie awake that night replaying the conversation?
qa.a: Uma felt uneasy that the first question had put Jaya on trial instead of the two men, which clashed with how Uma wanted to treat a friend.

qa.q: What did Uma choose to do the next morning, and why might it help Jaya?
qa.a: Uma apologised, told Jaya "They did this, not you," and helped with the police complaint, taking the blame off Jaya and giving practical help.

qa.q: What might Jaya have felt when she took her tea to her room?
qa.a: Jaya probably felt hurt and blamed, as if coming home shaken wasn't enough and she also had to defend herself 🥺.

grounding: The narrator catches a 'why did you let it happen' reaction to a robbery and shifts responsibility to the men who chose to act.

passage: Supervisor's note, Thursday. At today's shift review, Samir, our newest team lead, went through Tuesday's incident, when a delivery contractor shouted at Francis and shoved a crate at him. Samir began, "Why did Francis let it get that far? He could have walked off." Then he paused, looked at his notes, and said, "Actually, that's the wrong question. The contractor chose to shout. The contractor chose to shove the crate. What do we do about that?" The room shifted. Francis, who had kept his eyes on the table, looked up. The team agreed the contractor's firm will be informed, and loading will now have two staff present. Afterwards I thanked Samir for correcting himself in front of everyone. I also checked in with Francis privately; he said he felt heard. R. Kulkarni, shift supervisor

qa.q: What did the contractor do to Francis on Tuesday?
qa.a: A delivery contractor shouted at Francis and shoved a crate at him.

qa.q: What might Samir have realised when he paused over his notes?
qa.a: He seems to have realised that asking why Francis let it happen put the blame on the person harmed, when the contractor made the choices.

qa.q: Which decision at the review turned Samir's new question into action?
qa.a: The team agreed to inform the contractor's firm and keep two staff at loading, dealing with the person who acted rather than with Francis.

qa.q: How does Francis seem to experience the change in Samir's question?
qa.a: Francis, who had kept his eyes on the table, looked up, and later told R. Kulkarni that he felt heard.

grounding: A supervisor records a team lead replacing 'why did he let it happen' with who acted and what they chose.

passage:
Tuesday, late
Tushar came back from the client meeting grey in the face. The client, Mr Bedi, had thrown the printed report across the table and called Tushar 'useless' in front of three people.
First thing I thought, honestly: why did Tushar let him talk like that? Why not walk out? Why go alone?
I actually typed half of that into the chat before I stopped.
Tried the question the other way round. Who did something? Mr Bedi. What did he choose? To shout, to throw paper, to insult a junior in public. Tushar chose to stay calm and finish the meeting. That's the only choice on Tushar's side, and it wasn't a bad one.
Deleted my message. Sent: 'That was not okay of him. Want to tell our manager together tomorrow?'
Tushar replied: 'thanks Omkar, needed that 🙏'

qa.q: What did Mr Bedi throw across the table?
qa.a: The printed report.

qa.q: Why did 'why did Tushar let him' come to Omkar's mind first?
qa.a: It felt natural to look for what Tushar could have done differently; asking about the target's choices makes such things seem controllable and less frightening.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Omkar's evening, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Stopping halfway through typing and asking who acted and what they chose; Omkar deleted the blaming message and offered to go to the manager with Tushar.

qa.q: What would Tushar have felt if Omkar's first message had been sent?
qa.a: Tushar, already shaken, would likely have felt blamed a second time, as if the insult were Tushar's fault, and might have stayed quiet about it. 😔

grounding: An adult catches a 'why did they let it happen' thought about an insulted colleague and asks instead who acted and what they chose.

passage: The news reached the staffroom of the high school in Chalakudy at noon: a Class 9 girl had told her friend that the conductor on the morning bus kept brushing against her. Gopika heard herself say, 'Why does she always sit right by the door?' The words were out before she could stop them. She sat very still. Tushar, the maths teacher, looked at her. Gopika shook her head. 'No. Wrong question. She sat in a seat. He chose to touch her. The question is what he did, and what we do now.' She went with Tushar to the headmistress within the hour. The headmistress called the girl's parents and the bus depot that afternoon, and Gopika sat with the girl in the counsellor's room and told her, 'You did the right thing by telling. None of this is your fault.'

qa.q: What did the Class 9 girl say the conductor did?
qa.a: She said the conductor kept brushing against her on the morning bus.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel after hearing her own first question?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and ashamed of the question, which made her stop and rethink where the blame belonged.

qa.q: What did asking who acted change?
qa.a: It put responsibility on the conductor, and Gopika went straight to the headmistress, who contacted the parents and the bus depot that afternoon.

qa.q: How might the girl have felt hearing 'None of this is your fault'?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and believed, instead of blamed for where she sat.

grounding: A teacher catches herself asking why a girl sat by the door, then asks who acted and what he chose, returning responsibility to the one who caused harm.

passage: Rosa slid the letter across the café table in Berlin. The landlord was keeping her entire deposit for 'wear and tear' on a flat she had left cleaner than she found it. Selin read it and heard herself say, 'Why didn't you take photos when you moved in? Why did you let him get away with—' She stopped. Rosa's face had closed like a door. Selin put the letter down. 'Sorry. Wrong question. You didn't do anything. He decided to keep money that isn't his. That's on him.' Rosa's shoulders came down a little. 'So what do I do?' 'We look at what he chose and whether he's allowed to. There's a tenants' advice office near the station. Want to go tomorrow? I'll come.' Rosa nodded and finally picked up her coffee.

qa.q: What reason did the landlord give for keeping the deposit?
qa.a: He gave 'wear and tear' as the reason.

qa.q: Why did Selin stop mid-sentence?
qa.a: She saw Rosa's face close and felt a jolt of regret, realising her question was putting the blame on Rosa.

qa.q: What did Selin's corrected question lead to?
qa.a: Asking what the landlord chose put responsibility on him and led to a plan to visit the tenants' advice office together.

qa.q: How did Selin's first question feel to Rosa?
qa.a: It seemed to make Rosa feel blamed and ashamed, her face closing like a door.

grounding: An adult catches herself asking why her friend let it happen, then asks what the landlord chose, placing responsibility where it belongs.

passage: In the small HR office on the third floor, Gopika finished explaining: during the late shift, her team manager had shouted at her and grabbed her arm hard enough to leave marks. Aparna, two years into HR, felt the first question rise in her throat: why did you stay late alone with him? She swallowed it. She had once asked something like that and watched a colleague stop talking. Instead she asked, 'What did he do, exactly, and when?' She wrote it down: 9:40 p.m., shouted, grabbed left arm, marks visible. 'Thank you for telling me. None of this happened because of where you were standing. He chose to do it.' Gopika's eyes filled. Aparna called the head of HR while Gopika was still in the room; the head came down within ten minutes, moved Gopika to another floor from the next day, and started the formal complaint that afternoon.

qa.q: At what time did the manager grab Gopika's arm?
qa.a: He grabbed her arm at 9:40 p.m.

qa.q: Why did Aparna swallow her first question?
qa.a: She felt uneasy, remembering a colleague who stopped talking after a similar question, and recognised that it blamed Gopika for the harm.

qa.q: How did Aparna's question 'What did he do, exactly?' help?
qa.a: It focused on the manager's actions, produced a clear record, and let Aparna place responsibility with him before involving the head of HR.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel hearing 'He chose to do it'?
qa.a: She would likely feel believed and relieved, her eyes filling, because the blame was placed where it belonged.

grounding: An HR worker stops herself asking why a colleague stayed late and asks what the manager did, returning responsibility to him.

passage:
Subject: What I should have said

Mehak,

On Friday, when you told me the new manager had been calling you into his cabin late and making comments about your clothes, the first thing I said was, “Why did you keep going in alone?”

I've replayed that all weekend. It was the wrong question. It put the whole thing on you.

The right questions are: who made the comments? Who chose to call a junior into a cabin after hours? Who has the power to stop it? Those answers all point to him, not to you.

I'm sorry. You trusted me with this and I made you defend yourself.

If you want, I'll come with you to the internal committee on Monday, or sit with you while you write it down first. Whatever you decide, I'm on your side.

Arnab

qa.q: What did Arnab first ask Mehak on Friday?
qa.a: Arnab asked, “Why did you keep going in alone?”

qa.q: Why did Arnab replay the question all weekend?
qa.a: Arnab felt guilty and uncomfortable, realising the question put the responsibility on Mehak instead of on the manager.

qa.q: What makes Arnab's new questions a good countermeasure?
qa.a: Asking who made the comments, who called a junior in after hours and who has the power to stop it returns responsibility to the person who caused the harm.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt when Arnab asked about going in alone?
qa.a: Mehak likely felt blamed and ashamed, forced to defend a choice after trusting a friend.

grounding: The email shows an adult catching their own “why did you let it happen” question and asking instead who acted and what they chose.

passage:
So, you asked what changed how I talk to my team. It was one Tuesday, honestly.
I'm Jatin, I lead a small design team. Zeenat, one of our juniors, came to me upset. A senior from another team had presented her whole layout at the client meeting as his own. And the first thing out of my mouth was, “Why didn't you put your name on the file?”
She went quiet. I saw her shoulders drop. And I heard myself. I'd made her the one who had to explain.
So I stopped and said, “Sorry. Wrong question. Who presented it? Who knew it was yours and chose not to say?”
We went through it: he'd seen her drafts, he'd been told they were hers. That was a choice, and it was his.
I took it to his manager that afternoon, with her files. Now, whenever something goes wrong, I ask who acted first, before I ask who should have stopped them.

qa.q: What did the senior from another team present as his own?
qa.a: He presented Zeenat's whole layout at the client meeting as his own.

qa.q: What did Jatin feel when he heard his own first question?
qa.a: Jatin felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, noticing it made Zeenat the one who had to explain.

qa.q: Which change in Jatin's approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking who presented it and who chose not to say; it put the responsibility back on the senior, and taking the files to his manager the same afternoon backed that up.

qa.q: What is it like for Zeenat when her team lead asks why she didn't name the file?
qa.a: Zeenat feels dismissed and blamed, and her dropping shoulders show she felt the harm was being turned back on her.

grounding: The spoken account shows an adult catching a victim-blaming question and asking instead who acted, so responsibility returns to the one who caused the harm.

Bidisha came back from the client call pale. She said the client had shouted at her for ten minutes about a delay that came from their own side, and called her useless.

Monday. Over dinner, Ankita told Tanuja her team manager had shouted at her again in front of everyone, and made her stay till ten to redo a report. Tanuja's first words were, "Why do you let him do that?" Ankita put down her fork and didn't finish her food.
Wednesday. Tanuja kept thinking about her question. Why do you let him. As if Ankita were the one choosing. She wrote it differently in her head: who shouted? He did. Who decided she must stay till ten? He did. Who had the power in that room? Not Ankita.
Saturday. Tanuja sat with Ankita on the balcony. "I asked the wrong question on Monday. I'm sorry. He chose to shout. He chose to keep you late. What do you want to do?" Ankita let out a long breath. "I want to write it all down and take it to HR." "Then let's write it now." They started a list, with dates.

qa.a: Ankita felt hurt and blamed, putting down her fork and not finishing her food.

qa.q: What question did Tanuja learn to ask instead, and why is it better?
qa.a: Who acted and who had the power, because it puts responsibility back on the manager who shouted and kept Ankita late.

qa.a: Tanuja felt uneasy and regretful for days, until she found a better question and could support Ankita properly.

passage: Simran, you asked why your friend is upset with you. Let your Madhuri Mausi tell you something I learned late. When I was twenty-five, my closest friend Rekha rented a room from a landlord who kept her deposit and changed the locks while she was away. She came to me crying. And do you know what I said first? "Why did you give him the money without a receipt?" Her face closed like a door. She didn't call me for a week. At the time I thought I was being practical. But what I really did was make her the cause. When I finally went to her house, I said, "I'm sorry. I asked the wrong question. He chose to cheat you. He chose to change the locks." She cried again, but differently. We went to the tenants' help office together the next day. So when someone tells you they were hurt, beta, ask who acted, not what they did wrong.

qa.q: What did the landlord do while Rekha was away?
qa.a: He kept her deposit and changed the locks.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel after Madhuri's first question?
qa.a: Rekha felt blamed and hurt; her face closed like a door and she didn't call for a week.

qa.q: What choice in the story repaired the friendship?
qa.a: Madhuri going to Rekha's house, apologising, and saying plainly that the landlord chose to cheat her, then going to the tenants' help office together.

qa.q: Why might young Madhuri have asked about the receipt first?
qa.a: She may have felt helpless and wanted a practical answer, not seeing that it made Rekha the cause.

grounding: An aunt recalls asking a cheated friend why she let it happen, then learning to ask who acted and returning responsibility to the one who caused harm.

passage: It was pouring, the police station near the office closed at six, and Jomon was standing in the parking lot staring at the empty spot where his bike had been. Sharmila ran out with an umbrella. "Did you lock it?" she asked, before she could stop herself. Jomon's face fell. "The lock was broken. I was going to fix it this weekend." "Why would you leave it like that?" Then she heard herself. She took a breath. "Sorry. That's the wrong question. Somebody saw a bike and chose to steal it. That's on them." Jomon wiped rain off his face. "I still feel stupid." "You made a small mistake. They committed a crime. Those aren't the same size." She checked the time: forty minutes. "Come. We'll get the FIR done before they close. I'll drive." They reached the station at five-forty, soaked. The duty constable took the complaint and gave Jomon a copy.

qa.q: When did the police station close?
qa.a: The police station near the office closed at six.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel after Sharmila's first questions?
qa.a: Jomon felt stupid and blamed, his face falling when she asked if he'd locked it.

qa.q: What did Sharmila say that put responsibility back where it belonged?
qa.a: That somebody chose to steal the bike, and that a small mistake and a crime are not the same size.

qa.q: Why might Sharmila have asked about the lock first?
qa.a: In the rush and rain she reacted quickly, looking for a reason, before she noticed it made Jomon the cause.

grounding: Racing against time and rain, an adult catches herself asking why her colleague let his bike be stolen and asks instead who chose to act.

In the office canteen in Salt Lake, Salma told Arnab that Rituparna from her team had finally reported the senior manager who had been shouting at her in meetings for four months, calling her "useless" in front of clients.
"Four months?" Arnab said. "Why did she let it go on so long? She should have—" He stopped, spoon halfway to his mouth.

Salma nodded slowly. "That's what the HR head said too. They're looking into his conduct, not hers."
"Tell her I said she did a hard thing," Arnab said. "And that none of it was on her."
